t: Existence of a Substring in a String and Its Reverse
o: We need some length-2 substring of s that also occurs in reverse(s). In 'leetcode', 'ee' occurs in both s and 'edocteel' → true. In 'abcba', every adjacent pair reappears in the palindrome's reverse → true. In 'abcd', pairs are ab, bc, cd while reverse(s)='dcba' contains dc, cb, ba — no overlap → false. A key simplification: a pair p = s[i]s[i+1] occurs in reverse(s) iff the swapped pair s[i+1]s[i] occurs in s. So we only need two adjacent characters of s that mirror each other, which happens exactly when s[i] == s[i+1] or s[i] == s[i+2].
k: Pair (a,b) appears in both s and reverse(s) iff (b,a) also appears adjacently in s.
Therefore the answer is true iff ∃i with s[i]==s[i+1] or s[i]==s[i+2] — an O(n) check with no hashing needed.

a.i: Generate all length-2 substrings of rev = s[::-1] into a set, then test each length-2 substring of s for membership. Direct translation of the statement; with n ≤ 100 performance is irrelevant.
s: Insert every 2-character substring of rev into a hash set.
Scan s; if any 2-character substring is in the set, return true; otherwise false.
a.t: O(n) — building and probing the set of O(n) pairs.

a.i: As derived, a shared pair exists iff some character equals its neighbor at distance 1 or 2. Checking s[i]==s[i+1] covers palindromic pairs like 'ee'; checking s[i]==s[i+2] covers mirrored pairs like 'ab'…'ba'. This removes all data structures and is a one-liner.
s: For each i from 0 to n−3, test s[i]==s[i+1] or s[i]==s[i+2].
Also test the final adjacent pair s[n−2]==s[n−1].
a.t: O(n) — a constant number of comparisons per index.

w: Lead with the characterization if you can derive it live — it demonstrates understanding of why reversals flip adjacent pairs; otherwise the set approach is a safe, obviously-correct fallback. Pitfall: strings shorter than 2 have no pairs at all (answer false), and the distance-2 check must not read past the end. Follow-ups: generalize to substrings of length L (hash all length-L windows of s and of reverse(s)), or count how many distinct pairs are shared.
